I take it you are a fan could you tell me the pace of the book?

What do you mean by pace?

All Redwall books have a mix of fast paced action and slower paced, comfortable scenes (like feasts and hijinks around the abby). I'd recommend starting with Mossflower as it's the direct prequel to Redwall (even though written afterwards) and sets up Redwall very well.

So I grew up with these books, which is where my love for them stems from.

I think that's important because they aren't a very challenging read, so it may be tough for an adult to just pick up and become captivated by it. But the author writes in such simple yet vivid detail, which of course is conducive to young readers. Yet it also helps me regain my sense of imagination as an adult.

Your average Redwall book is going to introduce the good characters and the bad characters, have a lot of tasty food descriptions, some varying sense of adventure or questing, acts of heroism and cowardice, its general ups and downs before the end conclusion.

There's a hint of Medival-Christianity religious undertones to the books. It hasn't bothered me any, and I'm an atheist, mainly because the morals the books try to instill in the reader are just The Golden Rules (treat others the way you would like to be treated).

I'm 27 years old now, and what I get out of the most from these books is a sense of comfort. I can open one up, read a couple chapters, put it down and come back to it and just feel completely content.

I think the magic in these books is just the black and white world of good vs. evil. You can get lost in the beautiful descriptions of a healthy and vibrant world, and smile at the heroic mice/hares/otters/badgers who fight back at the evil rats/cats/foxes/stoats/weasels.

I definitely recommend it. Start with the series' namesake 'Redwall'. It was the first book he wrote and I recommend reading them all in the order in which he wrote them.

Edit: I would also like to thank you for coming by, there's always a place for you at Redwall Abbey
